opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a pretty humbling trajectory, honestly. When I started working on semantic parsing, the default assumption, mine included, was that you needed a lot of explicit structure: a grammar, some kind of compositional derivation, typed logical forms, maybe a lexicon you'd learned or hand-built. The model's job was to search over that space, and the structure was what made generalization possible.

Then sequence-to-sequence models came along, and with surprisingly little engineering you could take a pretty generic encoder-decoder, linearize your logical forms as strings, and get results competitive with, sometimes better than, the carefully structured systems on a lot of standard benchmarks. That forced a real reckoning. A lot of what we thought was necessary inductive bias turned out to be something a flexible model could pick up from data, at least on the distribution it was trained on.

But I don't think the lesson is just "structure doesn't matter." Where it gets interesting is out of distribution. When you test compositional generalization, recombining pieces you've seen in new ways, longer inputs, new combinations of primitives, the unstructured models often fall apart in ways structured models don't. So a lot of my thinking shifted from "how do I hard-code the right structure" to "what's the minimal bias, or the right data or training signal, that gets a flexible model to behave as if it had that structure when it matters." Some of our work on data augmentation came from that: rather than baking compositionality into the architecture, can you express it as a constraint on the data and let the model absorb it?

And with large pretrained language models, the picture shifted again. They've seen so much text that a lot of the structure we used to build in seems to be represented implicitly. Part of my research now is trying to find that structure inside the model, figuring out whether there's something like a compositional representation in there, and whether we can read it out or intervene on it.

So where I've landed is less a position on how much structure to build in, and more a belief that structure is still the right way to think about what these models need to do. The question has moved from the architecture to the representations, and to how we evaluate whether a model has really learned it versus pattern-matching around it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think my view has actually shifted quite a bit, and maybe not in the direction people would expect given the trajectory of the field.

When I started working on parsing, the dominant assumption was that structure was something you had to put in by hand. You'd write down a grammar, or at least a grammar formalism, you'd specify what the trees were allowed to look like, and then the learning problem was just estimating parameters for that fixed object. And the early neural parsing work I was involved in was sort of in that mold too: we'd keep the structured decoding algorithm, keep the trees, and just swap out the scoring function for a neural network.

What was striking, and a little humbling, was how much of the carefully designed structure turned out to be unnecessary for getting good numbers. You could throw away the grammar, do span-based prediction with a sequence encoder and a fairly simple decoder, and it worked as well or better. And then a few years later people showed you could get surprisingly far with no explicit tree structure at all, just sequence-to-sequence models that output bracketed strings. So the first lesson was: a lot of the structure we thought we needed as an inductive bias was really just compensating for weak feature representations. Once the representations got better, the scaffolding could come down.

But I don't think the right conclusion is "structure doesn't matter." I think the more interesting conclusion is that structure moved. It stopped being something you hardcode into the hypothesis class and became something you hope the model discovers, or something you impose through the data and the training objective, or something you use as an analysis tool after the fact to understand what the model learned. A lot of my own work since then has been about asking whether these models that were never given trees nonetheless end up representing something tree-like internally, and the answer is often "sort of, partially, in ways that are hard to pin down."

So where I've landed is something like this: structure is extremely valuable when you have little data or when you need guarantees about generalization, like compositional generalization to novel combinations. In the big-data regime it's much less clear that building it in helps, and it can actively hurt by forcing the model into a representation that doesn't quite match the problem. The real open question for me isn't "how much structure should I build in," it's "how do I get models to find the right structure on their own, and how do I check whether they did." That reframing is probably the biggest thing parsing taught me.

r002.rationale: It mentions sequence-to-sequence models that output bracketed strings, but does not identify linearizing trees and sequence prediction as the most effective approach.

astra-6.text:
I think it made me much less confident that the structure you want a model to produce has to be reflected explicitly in the architecture of the model itself. Parsing is a nice example because the output is a tree, and so it feels very natural to build a system whose computations also follow a tree, or that has a grammar built into it. But you can get surprisingly far by treating that tree as a sequence and training a fairly generic model to predict it.

The important qualification is that the structure hasn’t disappeared. It’s still present in the training data and in the way you represent the target. So the question becomes: where do you need to put that knowledge? Does it need to be in the architecture, or can the model learn it from examples?

That pushed me toward treating explicit structure as an empirical question. If you have a lot of data, a flexible model may learn the regularities you care about. If you have very little data, or you need to generalize in a particular way, building in some structure may still be valuable. I’m less interested now in whether a model looks like the linguistic theory we started with, and more interested in what that structure actually buys us.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s made me less confident that there’s a single right amount of structure to build in. With parsing, you have this very explicit account of what the output should look like—a tree—and historically we also built a lot of assumptions into the machinery that produced that tree. Neural models let us separate those two things. You can preserve a structured output while learning much more of the computation that gets you there.

The question then becomes: which parts of that structure are actually doing useful work? Something that helps when you have very little data might matter much less when you have a lot. And something that doesn’t improve accuracy on your standard test set might still help when you ask the model to generalize to unfamiliar combinations.

So I’ve moved toward thinking of structure as a hypothesis you should test, rather than something you either believe in or don’t. What does it buy you in terms of data efficiency, generalization, or control? And can you get those benefits with a weaker assumption? That feels like a more productive question than whether neural networks need syntax in some absolute sense.
